prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices interact to amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B040, with Kiyotaki and Moore as the only laureates. Round 1 did not weaken the core case. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) isolate one general mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral value feed back on asset prices, so small temporary shocks become large and persistent. It is a conceptual advance that has been absorbed into macroeconomic, financial and policy modelling over nearly three decades. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. The originating paper has two authors, every B040 proposal in the files names the same pair, and a single two-person part leaves no co-originator out and fits the three-person limit without an arbitrary cut. In answer to the chair's question about which criterion comes first: for a single part, I rank clarity of attribution and conceptual generality first, and maturity second. Direct empirical evidence matters, but I weigh it as a qualifier and not as the lead criterion. Several colleagues, including Dreber-Almenberg, Strömberg and Andersson, argue the citation should claim the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles and crises are modelled, not the size of the amplification. I have tightened my citation accordingly and I accept that framing. I also reconsidered the two-part idea of adding one B044 name to B040. I still reject it, because a one-name part would split the credit for the Autor-Dorn-Hanson design and misdescribe that achievement.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and some are not fully answered. First, the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises may be seen as having covered this territory. My distinction, that bank runs and deposit insurance differ from collateral-value feedback in the real economy, rests on my own reading and not on a verified comparison. Second, direct empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is more indirect than the theory's influence suggests, and the quantitative size of the effect is contested. That is the weakest point against B040 and it is exactly where B044 is strongest. Third, the contribution rests on essentially one seminal paper and its extensions, which some will judge narrow next to a broader empirical programme. Fourth, excluding Gertler and Gilchrist favours the originating theory over the more empirical financial-accelerator strand. As I wrote in round 1, that exclusion should rest on the independent origin of the mechanism and not on prior recognition of the accelerator. Finally, I am the chair, I am in the same broad field, and I am one of four B040 supporters. I do not treat support counts as merit, but I should not be the one to argue that B040 has momentum.

responses.point: Krusell moved from B002 to B044 in round 1. He now ranks B040 as an alternative and argues that the collateral-amplification mechanism has more indirect empirical validation and that the 2022 prize narrows its marginal novelty. He also says that leaving Dorn out of B044 would be hard to defend scientifically.
responses.response: I accept the Dorn point and I am updating on it. My opening alternative used Autor and Hanson only. If the committee goes to B044, I now think Autor, Dorn and Hanson is the defensible set, because the China-shock design is a three-author product. On B040 I still differ on weighting. The indirect empirical validation is real, but I do not think it outweighs a mechanism that reorganised how financial frictions are modelled, and influence on quantitative and policy models is the relevant test of durability. On the 2022 overlap, the specific difference is the object of analysis. The 2022 work concerned bank runs, deposit insurance and bank failures, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral values and asset prices feeding back on credit limits in the real economy. I cannot show that this fully answers the concern. It is a distinction of mechanism, not a verified claim about what the earlier prize covered, and I leave the rest to him and the other members to weigh.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B044 first with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, anchors the citation on empirical evidence on trade and technology exposure, and argues that a decade of replication refines the estimates without overturning the qualitative finding. He is unsure how large the B040 overlap with recognised financial-frictions work is.
responses.response: His argument that refinement without reversal is the right maturity test is fair, and it narrows the maturity gap I raised in round 1. I would no longer use shift-share inference as a decisive objection to B044. The remaining difference is attribution and scope, not quality. A citation anchored on trade-shock and local labour-market evidence, as he now frames it, is coherent for the three named authors. My preference for B040 turns on its cleaner origin and its longer scrutiny, not on a belief that the evidence for B044 is weak. I also accept his challenge on overlap. I cannot quantify how much of the financial-frictions territory earlier prizes cover, and I am not claiming it is zero. I only claim that the collateral-feedback mechanism is a separate object from what the 2022 prize described.

responses.point: Teorell moved from B017 to B044 on the strength of the overlap and attribution arguments. He proposes Autor, Dorn and Hanson, argues that a shared labour-demand question can support one citation, and says this is a judgement and still the main unresolved issue for B044.
responses.response: He is right that this is a judgement call, and I find his candour on it more useful than a firm claim either way. My concern from round 1 is that the task framework and the China-shock evidence have different lineages, with Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane and Katz in the first and Dorn in the second. A citation that implies both would credit three names with work that others share. If he keeps the citation on local labour-market adjustment to trade and technology exposure, as he says he would, that concern largely goes away. That is the one version of B044 in which I would be comfortable. B040 does not need that qualifier, which is why I still prefer it, but I would not describe the choice between the two as a clear scientific ranking.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first, dropped Katz in round 1 and now proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues that its direct identification is stronger than B040's more indirect validation, and she accepts that B040 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist.
responses.response: I agree with her on the trade-off. B040 has the cleanest attribution and B044 has the more direct evidence, and I do not think the committee can settle that by pointing to either strength alone. I do not accept that direct identification should outrank conceptual generality as a general rule, because a mechanism that restructured a field's models can be at least as consequential as a well-identified design. Her revision to drop Katz is the right one for coherence and it removes my earlier worry about a four-way credit boundary. I would put one question to her and the other B044 supporters. If the committee can only choose one achievement, would you prefer a prize that states its limits openly, crediting the mechanism and not the quantitative size for B040, or the empirical design and not the full technology-and-inequality literature for B044? I think both versions can be written honestly.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B040 first and says that the exclusion of Gertler and Gilchrist should not rest on prior recognition alone. He suggests that the stronger argument is a distinct empirical and quantitative strand, and that the committee should handle that on the merits if the distinctness is contested.
responses.response: I agree and I am keeping that position. My round-1 wording leaned too heavily on earlier recognition, and I have not independently verified how much of the accelerator strand any earlier prize covered. The exclusion is better argued on the independent origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism and on the cleaner two-person credit. I accept his point that Gertler and Gilchrist's work is a distinct empirical strand with its own merit, and that leaving it out is a cost, as Dreber-Almenberg also notes. I would state that cost openly if B040 advances. I would still not add names, because widening the credit would blur the origin of the mechanism and deepen the overlap question.

uncertainties: Whether the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises narrows the marginal case for Kiyotaki and Moore, and whether my distinction between bank-run theory and collateral-value feedback is persuasive to colleagues. I have not verified it beyond my own knowledge.
How much weight indirect empirical validation of the amplification mechanism should carry against conceptual generality and demonstrated influence on quantitative and policy models.

Whether the committee will treat the task-based framework and the China-shock evidence as one achievement or two, and whether a citation anchored only on trade-shock and local labour-market evidence is the right scope for B044.
Whether B040 and B044 can each be written honestly with explicit limits, and whether any single configuration can reach six votes given the present split of four and four.
Whether the exclusion of Gertler and Gilchrist understates the empirical side of the credit-friction literature.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and on the files supplied. I have not independently verified citation counts, attribution details or what earlier prizes covered.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I am the chair and one of four members who prefer B040. I work in macroeconomics, the same broad field as B040. My supplied profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Chetty, Hendren or any other credited name on the shortlist. I have co-authored with committee colleagues Boppart and Friberg, and with the secretary Krusell, who is also an IIES colleague. I am also an IIES colleague of Boppart. None of these ties concerns the credited names in my preferred configuration or my alternatives. My own climate-economics and political-economy work is not a candidate on the shortlist. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
